resources.string: Watches Instagram screens only. Blocks only the parts you switch on in the app.

Unscroll watches which Instagram screen is showing, so that it can keep you off the Reels tab and hide the Home feed and Explore, while leaving messages and posting alone.

It receives events from the Instagram app only. It reads the names and positions of on-screen elements, not message text. It taps the DMs tab for you and draws covers over parts of Instagram. A later version will also read usernames on Stories, only so that you can hide chosen people's Stories.

Every rule is off until you switch it on in the app, and the Unscroll tile in Quick Settings pauses everything.

The app has no internet permission.

Every blocking rule goes off, Stories go back on, and the hidden list, your username and the step-in counts are cleared. Inspector captures stay. This cannot be undone.
Its accessibility service switches off and Instagram works normally. To turn it back on, open Settings, then Permissions, then Open Accessibility settings.

One step-in is one visit to a blocked screen that Unscroll covered or left for you: the feed, Explore, the Reels tab, a reel from Explore or search, a result page. Counted on this phone only, for the last two weeks. It is a count, not a time estimate: Unscroll can\'t know how long you would have scrolled.
You open Instagram to see your friends\' Stories or reply to a message. An algorithm shouldn\'t take the rest of your time.

You open Instagram to see your friends' Stories or reply to a message. But the app is built to keep you there: the feed never ends, and the next swipe might always be the good one. Before you know it, the time is gone, and you never chose to give it.

Unscroll keeps what you came for: messages, Stories and posting. It removes the endless parts, so you get two things back: your time, and a clearer mind.

Why it matters: heavy scrolling through bad news (doomscrolling) is linked to more symptoms of depression and post-traumatic stress. Bright screens at bedtime worsen sleep, and attention on a screen now lasts about 47 seconds on average before we switch. And uncertain rewards, the kind a feed delivers, are especially good at engaging the brain's dopamine system.
Price et al., Psychological Trauma: Theory, Research, Practice, and Policy, 2022 · Chang et al., PNAS, 2015 · Mark, Attention Span, 2023 · Fiorillo, Tobler & Schultz, Science, 2003
Short summaries of published research. Results are averages across groups, not predictions for any one person.

string-array.name: science_texts
string-array.item: Dopamine neurons respond most strongly when a reward is uncertain: their sustained activity peaked when a reward came only half the time. An endless feed, where any swipe might be the good one, is built on that uncertainty.
Rewards that arrive after an unpredictable number of actions produce fast, persistent behaviour that is hard to stop. It is the schedule behind slot machines, and behind pull-to-refresh.

When teenagers saw their own photos with many likes, the nucleus accumbens, a core part of the brain\'s reward circuit, was more active. They were also more likely to like photos that already had many likes.

Students who limited Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat to 10 minutes each a day for three weeks reported significantly less loneliness and depression than a control group who used them as usual, most clearly in those who started out more depressed.

In a randomised experiment, people paid to deactivate Facebook for four weeks gained about an hour a day of free time and reported small but significant gains in well-being. Many kept using it less afterwards.
When phone use was logged instead of self-reported, young adults checked their phones around 85 times a day, about twice as often as they thought.
Switching away from a task leaves attention residue: part of your mind stays on the old task, and performance on the next one drops. Every quick look at a feed is a switch.
Logged on computers, people\'s attention on one screen now lasts about 47 seconds on average before they switch, down from about two and a half minutes in 2004.

Reading on a light-emitting screen before bed suppressed melatonin, delayed the body clock, made it take longer to fall asleep and left people less alert the next morning, compared with reading a printed book.

Texting young adults five times a day for two weeks showed that the more they used Facebook, the worse they felt at the next check-in, and the more their life satisfaction declined over the two weeks.
Left alone with their thoughts for 6 to 15 minutes, many people chose to give themselves mild electric shocks rather than do nothing. Reaching for a feed is often an escape from exactly that moment.
People randomly assigned to quit Facebook for one week reported higher life satisfaction and more positive emotions than those who kept using it, with the largest gains for heavy users.
Adults who took a one-week break from social media showed better well-being and less depression and anxiety than those who carried on as usual.

Observed while studying, students stayed on task for less than six minutes on average before switching, usually to technology. Those who checked Facebook during the session also had lower grade averages, a correlation rather than a proven cause.
People whose phone notifications arrived in three batches a day felt less stressed and more in control, and reported better attention and productivity, than those who got them as they came.
People who habitually juggle many media streams were worse at filtering out irrelevant information and slower at switching tasks than people who rarely do.
In a lab study, scrolling a stream of short TikTok-style videos left people worse at remembering to carry out a planned task than the comparison conditions did.

Over 30 days of daily check-ins during the COVID-19 pandemic, people reported more symptoms of depression and post-traumatic stress on days they used social media. It is a link, not proof of cause, and it was strongest for people who were already vulnerable.

resources.string: Unscroll runs beside the official Instagram app. It hides only the parts you switch off, such as Reels, the Home feed and Explore, and leaves messages, posting, your profile and Stories alone.

Android\'s accessibility service is the only way for an app to see which Instagram screen is showing and to cover parts of it. Unscroll reads the names and positions of Instagram\'s on-screen elements, never your messages.\n\nIt has no internet permission, and its covers need no \"display over other apps\" permission.
Easy to pause or turn off

Pause for a few minutes or until you resume, on the Focus tab or with one tap on the Unscroll tile in Quick Settings.\n\nTo turn it off completely, use Turn off Unscroll in Settings, or Android\'s Accessibility settings.
Two steps: switch on the accessibility service, and set battery use to Unrestricted. The Settings tab opens each page for you; you flip every switch yourself.
Explore hidden by Unscroll. Search for people above.
Each button opens a settings page. You flip the switches yourself; this app never changes phone settings.
Accessibility, then Installed apps, then Unscroll, then switch it on.
Open App info, tap the three dots at the top right, choose \"Allow restricted settings\", then repeat step 1. Usually only needed when the app was installed from a file on the phone.
Let it run in the background
In App info, tap Battery and choose Unrestricted, so your phone does not put the service to sleep.
Android 17\'s Advanced Protection removes accessibility access from apps like this one. Auto Blocker only matters when installing the app from a file on the phone.
The tile is already in Quick Settings.
Tile not added. You can also add it by editing Quick Settings.

Accessibility service: reads the structure of Instagram's screens, meaning the names and positions of on-screen elements. It taps the DMs tab or presses Back for you, and draws covers over the parts you switch off. It receives events from Instagram only.

Seeing that Instagram is installed: used to show its version. This is not a permission prompt.

Not requested: internet, display over other apps, usage access, notifications, contacts, storage, location.

With no internet permission, the app can't send anything on its own. The app's manifest in its source code lists every permission it asks for.
Switched on in Settings, but not running right now. Open Instagram once. If this does not change, switch the service off and on again.

Off. Switch on \"Unscroll\" in Accessibility settings. If your phone blocks it as a restricted setting, open App info for this app, tap the three dots, choose \"Allow restricted settings\", then try again.
